lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Here's what that means in a picture: a profile logistic log likelihood for the slope, reoptimizing the nuisance intercept at each slope. A fixed-intercept slice would understate uncertainty. <bookmark mark='b'/> In gold, the quadratic Newton fits at the top. <bookmark mark='c'/> Its curvature gives the standard error. <bookmark mark='d'/> The ninety-five percent Wald interval is where the quadratic has fallen by one point nine two, half of three point eight four, the chi-squared critical value. <bookmark mark='e'/> Using the real curve instead of its quadratic gives the likelihood-ratio interval, which can capture asymmetry under regular likelihood assumptions. Disagreement alone does not guarantee that its finite-sample coverage is better. Part 22 goes deeper.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> That gives a natural place to stop. Here's gradient ascent's distance from the exact maximum, falling as it runs. <bookmark mark='b'/> In gold, the estimate's standard error: the size of its statistical uncertainty. <bookmark mark='c'/> Once the optimization error is a tenth of that, after about a thousand iterations here, its magnitude is small on the statistical scale in this example. Numerical error need not be independent or mean-zero, so there is no general rule that it adds in quadrature or raises the standard error by half a percent. <bookmark mark='d'/> Going further computes more digits of a number we only know to plus or minus point one eight. <bookmark mark='e'/> Léon Bottou and Olivier Bousquet made this trade-off precise for large data in 2008: under an appropriate error-budget analysis, allocating computation to more data can be preferable to solving a smaller problem far more accurately than inference needs. In practice, the exact optimum is unknown: gradient, decrement or dual-gap criteria supply computable accuracy checks.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> The shape of the problem also warns us. A weakly curved regular direction can give a large standard error. An exactly flat, nonidentified direction instead invalidates the usual inverse-information approximation. <bookmark mark='b'/> A long ridge, like chapter five's, means strongly correlated estimates, which appropriate centring and scaling can reduce. In logistic regression, information uses fitted-probability weights; ordinary mean centring need not remove the correlation completely. <bookmark mark='c'/> Failure to converge can indicate nonidentification or a boundary, but poor scaling, initialization or an unsuitable algorithm can also cause it. <bookmark mark='d'/> In logistic regression, if a predictor separates the outcomes perfectly, the maximum is at infinity, and the iterations march off forever. <bookmark mark='e'/> The optimizer's struggles are diagnostics.
